Diagnoses: 

- Focal epilepsy with focal aware seizures and occasional focal to bilateral tonic-clonic evolution  
- History of childhood febrile seizures (resolved)  
- MRI brain (August 2025): Subtle left mesial temporal sclerosis  
- EEG (July 2025): Interictal left temporal sharp waves  

Current Medication: 

- Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd  
- Lacosamide 100 mg bd  
- Midazolam 10 mg buccal, as rescue for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) 

Plan: 

- Optimise anti-seizure medication: increase Lacosamide to 150 mg bd over two weeks if tolerated  
- Continue Levetiracetam 1,000 mg bd  
- Seizure diary to closely track frequency and potential triggers  
- Driving: patient not currently driving; to follow DVLA guidance and remain off driving until seizure-free per regulations  
- Consider referral to the epilepsy surgery MDT if disabling seizures persist despite optimisation  
- Safety advice provided regarding bathing, heights, hot surfaces, and nocturnal supervision  

I reviewed John in clinic today regarding focal epilepsy. He describes brief focal aware seizures characterised by rising epigastric sensation, déjà vu, and transient speech arrest, occasionally followed by right-hand automatisms and, more rarely, progression to bilateral tonic-clonic activity. He reports a current seizure frequency of 17 per month, typically clustering around periods of sleep deprivation and high work-related stress. He has found avoidance of alcohol helpful and is now using a structured sleep schedule. 

There is a remote history of childhood febrile seizures without neurological sequelae. Adult-onset focal seizures began in late 2023. Prior trials included Lamotrigine up to 200 mg bd, which was discontinued due to rash, and Carbamazepine up to 600 mg bd, which reduced frequency but caused significant dizziness and hyponatraemia; both medications were stopped in consultation with his previous team. 

We discussed treatment options. Given the MRI and EEG concordance suggesting a left mesial temporal focus, I have recommended optimising current therapy by titrating Lacosamide to 150 mg twice daily if tolerated, while continuing Levetiracetam 1,000 mg twice daily. He will maintain a detailed seizure diary and track potential triggers. A rescue plan using buccal Midazolam for prolonged seizures was reinforced. 

If disabling seizures persist at a rate similar to the current 17 per month despite dose optimisation and adherence, I will refer him to the epilepsy surgery multidisciplinary team for further evaluation, including consideration of prolonged video-EEG telemetry and neuropsychological assessment. We also reviewed DVLA regulations; he is not currently driving and understands requirements for resumption. 

I will review him again in three months, or earlier if there is any deterioration or adverse effects from the dose increase. 

With best wishes,

KINGS NEUROSCIENCES CENTRE


Clinic Date: 28 June 2016 

Dr Patel
Brookside Neurology Clinic

12 Brookside Way, London, SE5 9QT
Dear Dr Patel
Alex Morgan, DOB: 09-05-1987, Hospital No: NHS847362 NHS No. 7421936581
22A Elm Court, Brixton, London, SW2 1AB 

I reviewed the above patient in the Neurology Clinic today. Since their last appointment, they report predominantly nocturnal events observed by their partner; however, the partner was not present at today’s review. The patient keeps a diary and describes a pattern of seizures every seven days, with post-event morning headaches and tongue soreness on occasion. There is no reported injury, incontinence, or prolonged confusion, and there are no clear daytime triggers identified. They deny alcohol excess and have maintained regular sleep hours, though they note increased events during periods of shift work.

Current treatment is Lamotrigine 150 mg b.d. and Levetiracetam 1000 mg b.d. They report generally good tolerability, with intermittent irritability that they attribute to stress at work rather than medication. No rashes, visual disturbances, or gastrointestinal side effects are reported. Neurological examination today is unremarkable and observations are within normal limits.

We discussed strategies for documenting nocturnal events more reliably, including a bedroom audio alarm application and requesting their partner to record brief observations when safe to do so. The patient is agreeable to completing a two-week sleep and event diary to correlate with the seizure pattern. They are keen to avoid medication changes today and prefer to first optimise sleep hygiene and routine, which I have supported. I have requested an outpatient EEG with emphasis on sleep activation and will arrange a follow-up in three months, or sooner if the frequency increases beyond the current seizures every seven days or if any daytime events emerge.

Yours sincerely

Seizure disorder in the context of learning disability. 

Jamie Collins attended with their carer who assists with communication and seizure logging. The carer reports that seizures are occurring every 2 days on average, based on a written diary and a smartphone log that have been kept consistently since the last review. Plan: 
- Continue current antiseizure medication regimen as previously prescribed. 
- Maintain the seizure diary and smartphone log to corroborate the current pattern of every 2 days and to record any potential triggers, injuries, or use of rescue medication. 
- Provide short home video of typical events if safe to do so, to assist with further classification. 
- Community learning disability team to continue supporting communication strategies at appointments. 
- Safety advice reinforced around bathing supervision and cooking when fatigued; carer verbalised understanding. 
- We will arrange a follow-up in three months, or sooner if there is any escalation in frequency, prolonged events, or injuries. 

Yours sincerely

Centre for Epilepsy

Neurosciences Division 

Clinic Date: 01 June 2020 

Dr Priya Nair 
Consultant Neurologist  
Centre for Epilepsy  
Kingsway Community Hospital, London  

Dear Dr Priya Nair, 

Ms Aisha Rahman, DOB: 22-08-1992, Hospital No: K847203 NHS No. 9083175621  
Flat 12, 4 Brookside Close, London, SE15 3QH  

Diagnosis: 

Combined generalised and focal epilepsy. The patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy, with generalised tonic–clonic seizures occurring from sleep and focal aware auras occasionally progressing to focal impaired awareness events.

Aetiology: 

No definitive structural lesion identified on MRI; family history of seizures in a first-degree relative reported. EEG with mixed features including generalised spike–wave and independent right temporal sharp activity.

Other Medical Problems: 

Mild asthma on inhaled corticosteroid as required. Vitamin D insufficiency previously treated, currently stable.

Management Plan: 

- Continue sodium valproate modified-release 500 mg mane and 1,000 mg nocte.  
- Maintain clobazam 10 mg nocte as adjunct for nocturnal generalised seizures.  
- Rescue plan discussed: buccal midazolam 10 mg for prolonged generalised tonic–clonic seizure (>5 minutes) or seizure clustering, with instructions provided to family.  
- Driving advice reiterated in accordance with DVLA guidance for combined seizure types; patient has self-declared and remains off driving pending seizure control.  
- Lifestyle: reinforce regular sleep, hydration, and avoidance of known precipitants (patient-reported missed meals and sleep deprivation).  
- Review in four months with repeat trough valproate level and LFTs prior to clinic; consider lacosamide add-on if focal impaired awareness events persist.

Clinical Summary: 

Since the last review, Ms Aisha Rahman reports that events tend to cluster every seven to nine days. On those days, they experience a brief focal aware aura described in their own words as a “tight, metallic taste with a rising flutter in the stomach and a momentary pull to the right side,” lasting 10–20 seconds. They have practiced aura recognition strategies previously and now routinely sit down, slow their breathing, and alert a family member when the warning occurs. This has reduced secondary generalisation on several occasions. Over the same interval, there have been two nocturnal generalised tonic–clonic seizures, each under two minutes, with typical post-ictal confusion and myalgia but no injury. Daytime focal impaired awareness episodes are rare and usually follow the described warning if they cannot implement their strategy in time.

No adverse effects from current medication are reported beyond mild morning sedation, which is acceptable to the patient. Weight is stable; mood is good without features of depression or anxiety. There is no new neurological deficit on examination. We discussed trigger recognition and the patient prioritised consistent sleep and regular meals; they have set phone reminders and are keeping a seizure diary correlating auras, full seizures, and potential triggers. Family have been re-educated in the rescue plan and recovery position.

I will continue to support their self-management approach, given the usefulness of early warning recognition in reducing generalisation. No further investigations requested today beyond routine blood monitoring for valproate. I have provided a work letter confirming variable fatigue every seven to nine days corresponding to their seizure pattern and the need for flexible start times after nocturnal events.

Yours sincerely

I reviewed the above patient in the Adult Neurology Clinic today following transition from paediatric services. A parent attended and contributed helpful collateral history. He has a confirmed diagnosis of generalised epilepsy.

This is our first adult clinic review post-transition. From the joint handover summary and today’s history, his typical episodes comprise brief staring spells with eyelid flutter and occasional myoclonic jerks shortly after waking. Generalised tonic–clonic seizures have been infrequent. At present he reports clusters of brief absence episodes every 4 weeks, usually over 1–2 days, often precipitated by reduced sleep and academic stress. His last generalised tonic–clonic seizure was in May 2025 after a night of sleep deprivation, and there have been none since.

He describes mild morning lethargy and intermittent low mood around examination periods, which he and his parent feel are manageable. No rashes, visual disturbance, or focal neurological symptoms were reported. There is no history of focal onset phenomena. He is not driving.

Paediatric EEGs have shown generalised spike–wave discharges, most recently in 2024. MRI brain (2023) was normal. We will arrange an updated EEG to reassess background and interictal activity in the adult service and to support ongoing management planning. Given his current pattern of absence clusters every 4 weeks without recent convulsions, I have not altered medication today. We discussed adherence, regular sleep, and stress management as practical measures that may help reduce breakthrough events. He and his parent were given information on our transition nurse specialist and epilepsy advisor should they wish to discuss education or lifestyle issues further.

I have asked him to keep a simple seizure diary, noting any absence clusters and possible triggers, particularly sleep loss. We will review him in 6 months, or sooner if events increase in frequency, if he experiences any adverse effects, or if a generalised tonic–clonic seizure recurs.

Yours sincerely
